--- title: "Where in the Waters?" description: "Geospatial Analysis for Aquacultures on the West Coast" affiliation: - University of California, Santa Barbara - Masters of Environmental Data Science at the Bren School affiliation-url: https://bren.ucsb.edu/masters-programs/master-environmental-data-science date: 12-02-2026 format: html: toc: true toc-depth: 3 code-fold: true code-summary: "Show code" categories: [Aquaculture, Data Science, Geospatial, R] image: images/aqua.jpg editor_options: chunk_output_type: inline --- ![](images/image_aqua.avif) # Background ## What is the Future of Food Security? Marine aquaculture has the potential to be a more sustainable option to create future food security than the alternative land-based approach as the rising human population is estimated to reach 10 billion by 2050 (Gentry et al, 2017). Traditional farming is highly resource intensive. Beef production uses 61.1kg of grain and 28 kg for pork production, while 1 kg of finfish would use less than 13.5 kg of grain (Hall et al. 2011). Despite the promising solution, there is very little known about the areas on where species can thrive and aquacultures can succeed. Gentry et al. calculated the growth performance index and spatially assessed the location for general growing potential for suitable fish and bivalves (2017). ## Why the Ocean? The Earth’s living space is represented by 99% of water by volume and the ocean contains 97%. For this reason, the United Nations has implemented a Sustainable Development Goal 14 (Life Below Water) to include ocean conservation and encourage marine resources to be utilized efficiently (2022). This also ties into other United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals 1 (No poverty) and 2 (Zero hunger). Marine aquaculture seeks to meet the protein demands with the ocean representing an opportunity for food production with its potential being regarded as mostly untapped in terms of a farming source(Gentry et al. 2017). # Research Question This analysis determines the suitable locations along the west coast for several oyster species and blue mussel using Exclusive Economic Zones(EEZ). EEZ is an area that extends roughly 230 miles beyond a nation's territorial sea which is a boundary on where costal nations have jurisdiction over all resources, living and non-living (NOAA, 2020). **Where on the West Coast could oysters develop in aquaculture?** **Where on the West Coast could blue mussels develop in aquaculture?** Suitable growing conditions are dependent on sea surface temperature and ocean depth for species' optimal growth. | Species | Depth | Sea Surface Temperature | | --- | --- | --- | | Oyster | 0 - 70 meters below | 11- 30 °C| | Blue Mussel | 0 - 60 meters below | 5 - 20 °C | Blue mussels, *Mytilus edulis*, are eurythermal and well adapted to temperatures of 5–20 °C, with an upper thermal tolerance limit of about 29 °C for adults (Matoo et al. 2021). The depth for blue mussels was found on the website [SeaLifeBase](https://www.sealifebase.ca/search.php) and the oyster's information was given by the instructor. ## Set-up The geospatial analysis ues a few packages to create a function for mapping out the suitable locations throughout the West Coast region, which uses the following: - `tidyverse`: R package for syntax and data structures - `sf`: Simple features represents all types of common vector geometry - `tmap`: Thematic maps handles vector and raster objects with ggplot grammar - `terra`: For spatial data analysis - `kableExtra`: to make nice HTML tables ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} library(tidyverse) library(sf) # vector data library(here) library(tmap) # static or interactive maps library(janitor) library(terra) # spatial data library(kableExtra) # tables ``` ::: ## Data The table represents the datasets that are used throughout this analysis in order to discover the locations for potential aquaculture in the West Coast region. | Dataset | Description | Source | | --- | --- | --- | | Bathymetry (depth) | Charecterize the depth of the ocean | [General Bathymetric Chart of the ceans](https://www.gebco.net/data-products/gridded-bathymetry-data#area) | | Exclusive Exonomic Zones (West Coast Region) | Martitime boundaries use for the creation of species distribtion lists per country | [Marine Regions](https://www.marineregions.org/eez.php) | | Average Annual Sea Surface Temperature| from the years 2008 to 2012 within the region| [NOAA](https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/product/5km/index_5km_ssta.php)| ### Load and inspect data The sea surface temperature (SST) came from NOAA in multiple data files from 2008 to 2012. The data files were individually loaded then stacked to create a single raster file. The other two files were simply read accourdingly. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} # Read in data for the average SST set_file <- c( here("posts", "2026-11-26-aquaculture", "data", "average_annual_sst_2008.tif"), here("posts", "2026-11-26-aquaculture", "data", "average_annual_sst_2009.tif"), here("posts", "2026-11-26-aquaculture", "data", "average_annual_sst_2010.tif"), here("posts", "2026-11-26-aquaculture", "data", "average_annual_sst_2011.tif"), here("posts", "2026-11-26-aquaculture", "data", "average_annual_sst_2012.tif") ) # File path for SST data stack sst <- rast(set_file) # Load bathymetry data depth <- rast(here("posts", "2026-11-26-aquaculture", "data", "depth.tif")) # Load West Coast EEZ eez_data <- sf::st_read(here("posts", "2026-11-26-aquaculture", "data", "wc_regions_clean.shp")) ``` ::: The average sea surface temperature over the 5 year period was calculated and converted from Kelvin to Celsius. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # single raster of average SST sst_mean_c <- mean(sst, na.rm = TRUE) - 273.15 ``` ::: Depth and SST had different extents, resolutions, and origins, which were redefined using `resample()` and `crop()` for proper alignment. Two different CRS between the three datasets: - `depth`: EPSG 4326 - `sst`: EPSG 9122 - `eez_data`: EPSG 9122 Since there were two datasets with the same CRS, the choice to change `depth` to match the others was decided. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Crop data to match SST raster crop_depth <- crop(depth, sst_mean_c) # Transfer sst data using bilear method to match resampled_depth <- resample(crop_depth, sst_mean_c, method = "bilinear") # test if the resampled depth CRS matches the sst_mean_c CRS if (crs(resampled_depth) == crs(sst_mean_c)) { print("CRS match!") } else { warning("CRS don't match!") crs(resampled_depth) <- crs(sst_mean_c) } ``` ::: ## Suitable location workflow The following five steps are to build a function that will be used later to find suitable locations for marine species based on their sst and depth requirements. ### Step 1. Reclassifying based on conditions Both sst and depth were reclassified into 0's and 1's coinciding suitability of locations by creating a reclassification matrix. Rows in the matrix are as following: - outside the lower range receive 0 - suitable condition within range receives 1 - outside the higher range recieve 0 ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Variables for min and max SST min_sst <- 11 max_sst <- 30 # SST reclassification matrix rcl_sst <- matrix( c( -Inf, min_sst, 0, min_sst, max_sst, 1, max_sst, Inf, 0 ), ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE ) # Variables for min and max depth min_depth <- 0 max_depth <- -70 # Depth reclassification matrix rcl_depth <- matrix( c( -Inf, max_depth, 0, max_depth, min_depth, 1, min_depth, Inf, 0 ), ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE ) # Reclassify sst and depth to suitable zones zone_sst <- classify(sst_mean_c, rcl = rcl_sst) zone_depth <- classify(resampled_depth, rcl = rcl_depth) # Combine to adhere to satisfy both sst and depth for suitable zones depth_sst_zones <- c(zone_sst, zone_depth) ``` ::: ### Step 2. Combine with map algebra After reclassification, a function for map alegbra using `lapp()` to layers as arguments. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} zone_fun <- function(sst, depth){ sst * depth } # Find suitable zones for oysters adhering to both conditions suitable_zones <- lapp(depth_sst_zones, fun = zone_fun) ``` ::: ### Step 3. Rasterize EEZ regions EEZ data was rasterized by Region ID. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Convert to raster eez_raster <- rasterize(eez_data, suitable_zones, field = "rgn_id") ``` ::: The EEZ raster values 1 through 5 are assigned as the following: 1. Oregon 2. Northern California 3. Central California 4. Southern California 5. Washington ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(eez_raster, axes = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Exclusive Economic Zones on the West Coast](index_files/figure-html/Plotting EEZ-1.png){width=384} ::: ::: ### Step 4. Calculate the suitable areas within each EEZ region Before moving onto any other spatial operations, `cellSize()` was used to compute the true area (km^2) of each cell to determine the suitable locations within EEZ. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Calculate cell size cell_size <- cellSize(suitable_zones, unit = "km", mask = TRUE) ``` ::: Then set values to 0 that are outside the boundary and use only cells with value 1 to determing the suitable locations using `mask()`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Use only the cells with value 1 as suitable in the total area suitable_zmask <- mask(cell_size,suitable_zones, maskvalues = 0) ``` ::: Use the `zonal()` operation to apply the sum of area using the EEZ raster and the masked suitable zones. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Select raster cells by suitable zpmes inside EEZ desired_zone <- zonal(suitable_zmask,eez_raster, fun = 'sum', na.rm = TRUE) ``` ::: A table was created to show the total suitable area found inside EEZ for oysters. ::: {.cell tbl-cap='Suitable area (km^2) in EEZ by region'} ```{.r .cell-code} desired_zone |> kable(col.names = c("EEZ region", "Suitable area (km^2)")) |> kable_styling(bootstrap_options = "striped") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
EEZ region Suitable area (km^2)
1 1395.7328
2 323.9124
3 4373.5565
4 3329.9002
5 3091.5158
````` ::: ::: ### Step 5. Join results to EEZ regions and map suitable location Before mapping, the suitable areas are inputted into a tibble to the `left_join()` with EEZ. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Create a tibble z_tibble <- as_tibble(desired_zone) # Merge for desired zones to EEZ data map_1 <- left_join(eez_data, z_tibble, by = "rgn_id") ``` ::: A simple color palette was created for an aesthetically pleasing map of the West Coast. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Creating a color palette to differentiate the regions color_palette <- c("#d0f0f0", "#5fb3c7", "#1f78a8", "#08306b") ``` ::: The first map for the oyster was confirmed to be accurate to the suitable locations determined by EEZ, though it is not shown here but instead shown further ahead. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Visualize oyster suitable area by EEZ region tm_basemap("OpenStreetMap") + tm_shape(map_1) + tm_polygons( fill = "area", fill_alpha = 0.7, col = "grey30", fill.scale = tm_scale_continuous(values = color_palette), fill.legend = tm_legend( title = "Suitable Area (km²)", position = tm_pos_out("right", "center") ) ) + tm_text(text = "rgn_key", size = 0.7, col = "grey20") + tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2, position = c("right", "top")) + tm_scalebar(position = c("left", "bottom"), size = 5) + tm_options(component.autoscale = FALSE) + tm_title("Suitable Oyster Aquaculture\nin the West Coast by EEZ", size = 1) ``` ::: A table was created to show the suitable areas from the total area available inside EEZ by region. This depicts that only a small portion of areas inside suitable regions meet the criteria for both sea surface temperature and depth with the highest being 2.2% suitability in Central California. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Create a table for area by region and suitability map_1 |> st_drop_geometry() |> select(rgn_id, area, area_km2) |> arrange(desc(area)) |> mutate(pct_suitable = area / area_km2 * 100) |> kable( digits = 1, col.names = c( "EEZ Region", " Suitable Area (km²)", "Total EEZ Area (km²)", "Suitable (%)" ), caption = "Oyster Aquaculture by Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) in the West Coast", booktabs = TRUE ) |> kable_styling(latex_options = c("striped", "hold_position")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Oyster Aquaculture by Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) in the West Coast
EEZ Region Suitable Area (km²) Total EEZ Area (km²) Suitable (%)
3 4373.6 202738.3 2.2
4 3329.9 206860.8 1.6
5 3091.5 66898.3 4.6
1 1395.7 179994.1 0.8
2 323.9 164378.8 0.2
````` ::: ::: # Function: Find Suitable Area for Marine Species The function is called after EEZ species and used as shown: `eez_species(min_sst, max_sst, min_depth, max_depth, species_name)` The function utilizes the five steps detailed above and creates a map or a table for the given species by inputting the following: - minimum and maximum SST - minimum and maximum depth - "species name" ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} eez_species <- function( min_sst, max_sst, min_depth, max_depth, species_name ){ # Step 1. SST matrix reclassification rcl_sst <- matrix( c( -Inf, min_sst, 0, min_sst, max_sst, 1, max_sst, Inf, 0 ), ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE ) # Reclassify SST zone_sst <- classify(sst_mean_c, rcl = rcl_sst) # Reclassify depth rcl_depth <- matrix( c( -Inf, max_depth, 0, max_depth, min_depth, 1, min_depth, Inf, 0 ), ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE ) zone_depth <- classify(resampled_depth, rcl = rcl_depth) # Combine the two zones together depth_sst_zones <- c(zone_sst, zone_depth) # Step 2. Define function zone_fun <- function(sst, depth){ sst * depth} # Find suitable zones suitable_zones <- lapp(depth_sst_zones, fun = zone_fun) # Step 3. Convert to raster eez_raster <- rasterize(eez_data, suitable_zones, field = "rgn_id") # Step 4. Calculate cell size cell_size <- cellSize(suitable_zones, unit = "km", mask = TRUE) # Keep cell area only where suitable areas equals 1 suitable_zmask <- mask(cell_size,suitable_zones, maskvalues = 0) # Use zonal function to sum masked result and eez raster desired_zone <- zonal(suitable_zmask,eez_raster, fun = 'sum', na.rm = TRUE) # Step 5. Create tibble z_tibble <- as_tibble(desired_zone) # Merge for desired EEZ regions map <- left_join(eez_data, z_tibble, by = "rgn_id") # Create color palette color_palette <- c("#d0f0f0", "#5fb3c7", "#1f78a8", "#08306b") # Visualize EEZ map_species <- tm_basemap("OpenStreetMap") + tm_shape(map) + tm_polygons( fill = "area", fill_alpha = 0.85, col = "grey30", fill.scale = tm_scale_continuous(values = color_palette), fill.legend = tm_legend( title = "Suitable Area (km²)", position = tm_pos_out("right", "center") ) ) + tm_text(text = "rgn_key", size = 0.7, col = "grey20") + tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2, position = c("right", "top")) + tm_scalebar(position = c("left", "bottom")) + tm_options(component.autoscale = FALSE) + tm_title(paste0("Suitable ", species_name, " Areas by EEZ in the West Coast"), size = 1) # Create a table table <- map |> select(rgn_id, area, area_km2) |> arrange(desc(area)) |> mutate(pct_suitable = area / area_km2 * 100) |> st_drop_geometry() return(list(map_species, table)) } ``` ::: # Results ## Osysters For oyster species, inputting: - 11- 30 (°C) - 0 - 70 (meters) - Oysters ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Verify function by using oysters oyster <- eez_species(11, 30, 0, -70, 'Oysters') oyster[[1]] ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Map of the West Coast showcasing the suitable areas that meet several oyster's requirements for aquaculture possibilites based on Exclusive Economic Zones.](index_files/figure-html/map for oyster-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: ::: {.cell tbl-cap='Table depicting the total area (Km^2) by EEZ regions in the West Coast for several oyster species.'} ```{.r .cell-code} # Make a table for blue mussel knitr::kable(oyster[[2]], digits = 2, col.names = c("EEZ Region", " Suitable Area (km²)", "Total EEZ Area (km²)", "Suitable (%)")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | EEZ Region| Suitable Area (km²)| Total EEZ Area (km²)| Suitable (%)| |----------:|--------------------:|--------------------:|------------:| | 3| 4373.56| 202738.33| 2.16| | 4| 3329.90| 206860.78| 1.61| | 5| 3091.52| 66898.31| 4.62| | 1| 1395.73| 179994.06| 0.78| | 2| 323.91| 164378.81| 0.20| ::: ::: The best EEZ region for oysters is in Central California with 2.16% of the total area being suitable and 1.61% within Southern California ## Blue mussels For blue mussels, inputting: - 5 - 20 (°C) - 0 - 60 (meters) - Blue Mussels ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Use function for blue mussel blue_mussels <- eez_species(5, 20, 0, -60, 'Blue Mussel') blue_mussels[[1]] ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Map of the West Coast showcasing the suitable areas that meet the Blue Mussel's requirements for aquaculture possibilites based on Exclusive Economic Zones.](index_files/figure-html/map for blue mussel-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: ::: {.cell tbl-cap='Table depicting the total area (Km^2) by EEZ regions in the West Coast for Blue Mussel species.'} ```{.r .cell-code} # Make a table for blue mussel knitr::kable(blue_mussels[[2]], digits = 2, col.names = c("EEZ Region", " Suitable Area (km²)", "Total EEZ Area (km²)", "Suitable (%)")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | EEZ Region| Suitable Area (km²)| Total EEZ Area (km²)| Suitable (%)| |----------:|--------------------:|--------------------:|------------:| | 5| 6545.83| 66898.31| 9.78| | 3| 3910.14| 202738.33| 1.93| | 1| 3152.90| 179994.06| 1.75| | 4| 2938.33| 206860.78| 1.42| | 2| 2410.14| 164378.81| 1.47| ::: ::: The best EEZ region for blue mussels is in Washington with 9.78% of the total area being suitable and 1.93% within Central California # Discussion The different requirements per species resulted in different suitable geographic regions on the West Coast. The blue mussels are inclined to colder waters, such as those found in Washingoton, while oysters are inclined to slightly warmer waters, from Central to Southern California, for optimal growth. A limitation that may impact these results can come from the sea surface temperature data ranging from 2008 to 2012, which may need to be expanded in order to capture the patterns of annual or seasonal changes, expecially within the 2020's as there have been numerous record breaking temperatures. For blue mussels, warming waters affects growth not ocean acidification (OA) though the study was limited to adults excluding larval stage (Matoo et al. 2021). OA may not be a factor into blue mussel growth, but there could be others that could increase or decrease the suitable zones beyond temperature and depth. The ocean can be limited by national jurisdiction by the military or even energy production which reduces the available space for aquaculture (Gentry et al. 2017). ## Future direction 1. **Demands:** High demands on resources can intensify animal farming and inputs such as energy or ecosystem services like nutrient cycling (Hall et al. 2011). 2. **Development:** To further understand future development of marine aquaculture across the world, research and policy development is needed on the integration of growth potential with economic and social aspects that coincide with aquaculture (Gentry et al. 2017). 3. **Consideration:** Several communities are dependent on traditional fisheries and would benefit from consideration by integrating social, political, cultural, ecological dimensions into aquaculture planning where policymakers can practice expansion rather than replacement and support an equitable and sustainable seafood future (). # References Gentry, R.R., Froehlich, H.E., Grimm, D. et al.
